Drinking Water · Delaware

Is my water safe?

Find your public water system and read its drinking water record from EPA: every violation, its dates, and whether the state recorded it as resolved. All 1,362 systems Delaware regulates, as retrieved October 14, 2026.

How to read this. These are violations recorded in EPA's Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) for the public water systems Delaware regulates, shown without interpretation. A health-based violation means a contaminant went over a federal limit or a required treatment step was not met; most other violations are tests or reports that were missed or late. A returned to compliance date means the state recorded the violation as resolved. A past violation does not describe the water today. Systems are listed alphabetically; we rank none of them. EPA's data syncs about every three months, so a very recent violation may not appear yet. Lead service lines are covered separately below. First State Lens draws no conclusions. We show you the data; you decide.

What these records can and cannot tell you

START HERE

No website can tell you whether the water in your glass is safe right now. Two public records help you judge for yourself. Your water system's yearly water quality report, the Consumer Confidence Report, lists what was found in your water and the federal limit for each contaminant. EPA's violation record, on this site, shows when your system broke a drinking water rule and whether the state recorded the problem as resolved.

  1. Find your water supplier's name on your water bill.
  2. Find that system in the list below and open its page.
  3. Get its yearly water quality report from your supplier. EPA explains how to find and read it.
  4. For questions, contact your supplier or Delaware's Office of Drinking Water. The state also publishes system records in Drinking Water Watch.

On a private well? A private well is not a public water system, so it is not in these records. The Division of Public Health has information for private well owners.

What the terms mean

EPA DEFINITIONS
Community water system
Serves the same people year-round where they live, such as a town, a utility or a manufactured home community.
Non-transient non-community water system
Serves at least 25 of the same people for at least six months a year where they are not living, such as a school or a workplace.
Transient non-community water system
Serves people who do not stay long, such as a restaurant, a gas station or a campground.
Maximum contaminant level (MCL)
A contaminant was measured above its federal limit.
Treatment technique (TT)
A required treatment step or process was not met.
Monitoring and reporting (MR, MON, RPT)
A required test or report was missed or late.
Returned to compliance
The state recorded the violation as resolved, on the date shown.

Source: EPA drinking water regulations and contaminants and EPA SDWIS overview.
